chapter_note.about: Linear algebra and machine learning both run on lists and grids of numbers. This chapter rebuilds seven tools: vectors as arrows and lists, adding and scaling, length, the dot product, matrix times vector, matrix times matrix, and the identity and transpose. Every idea comes with a picture or grid you can redraw on paper, and every computation is done by hand. These tools feed linear algebra directly (systems, eigenvalues, projections) and machine learning (features, weights, layers).
chapter_note.simple: A vector is a list of numbers that you can also picture as an arrow: the list (3, 2) means go 3 steps right and 2 steps up. You add two arrows by walking one and then the other, and you stretch one by multiplying every number in it. The dot product multiplies matching numbers of two lists and adds them up, and it comes out as zero when the arrows are at right angles. A matrix is a grid of numbers that acts on a vector: each row of the grid takes a dot product with the vector. Multiplying two matrices repeats that for every column. The identity matrix does nothing, and the transpose flips the grid so that rows become columns.

Multiplying two small matrices, finding one entry of a product, and powers of a matrix are the typical 1- and 2-mark questions. Foundation, used in: la.matrices_det, la.systems_rank, la.eigen.
Predictions in machine learning are dot products and matrix-vector products: $\hat y=w\cdot x$, and a layer is $Wx+b$. Foundation, used in: ml.linreg, ml.ffnn, ml.pca.

cards.title: Vectors: arrows and lists
cards.simple: A vector is a list of numbers that you can also draw as an arrow. Think of directions to a friend's house: 'walk 3 blocks east, then 2 blocks north'. The list (3, 2) says exactly that, and the arrow is the straight path from where you started to where you end up. A list of three numbers is an arrow in a room, with left-right, front-back and up-down. Your marks in three subjects are also a list of three numbers, even though you cannot walk along them. In exam words: a vector in ℝⁿ is an ordered list of n real numbers called components, and geometrically it is an arrow from the origin to the point with those coordinates.
cards.idea: A **vector** is an ordered list of numbers, such as $(3,2)$. Drawn on a grid, it is an arrow from the origin: 3 steps right, then 2 steps up. The list has one number per direction, so $(3,2)$ lives in a plane and $(2,5,1)$ lives in 3-D space. In data work, a vector is simply one row of measurements.
cards.definition:
$$v=(v_1,v_2,\dots,v_n)\in\mathbb R^n$$

$v_1,\dots,v_n$ are the **components** (the numbers in the list) and $n$ is the **dimension** (how many numbers). Order matters: $(3,2)\ne(2,3)$. The vector from point $P$ to point $Q$ is $Q-P$, component by component. The zero vector $\mathbf 0=(0,\dots,0)$ is the arrow that goes nowhere.
cards.intuition_full: There are two pictures and you need both. The arrow picture helps you see direction, length and angles. The list picture lets you (or a computer) do the arithmetic, and it still works in 100 dimensions where no arrow can be drawn. They are the same object: the list is the set of instructions for drawing the arrow. An arrow can start anywhere. What defines the vector is the change it describes, how far in each direction, so the arrow from (1,1) to (4,3) and the arrow from the origin to (3,2) are the same vector. To find the vector between two points, subtract the start from the end. In machine learning, a house with area 80, 2 bedrooms and age 10 is the vector (80, 2, 10), and everything else in this chapter is how to compute with such lists.

examples.setup: Draw the vector $v=(3,2)$ and write it as a list.
steps: Start at the origin. The first component, 3, says how far to move right.
The second component, 2, says how far to move up from there.
The straight arrow from the origin to the end point is the vector $v$.
As a list it is $[3,\,2]$: the same information as the arrow, written as numbers.

examples.setup: Points are $P=(2,5)$ and $Q=(6,1)$. Find the vector from $P$ to $Q$ and say how far it moves in each direction.
steps: The vector from $P$ to $Q$ is $Q-P$: subtract start from end, component by component.
So $\overrightarrow{PQ}=(4,-4)$: 4 right and 4 down. The minus sign means down.

examples.setup: Is the arrow from $(1,1)$ to $(4,3)$ the same vector as the arrow from the origin to $(3,2)$? And what kind of vector is $(2,-1,4)$?
steps: That is the same list, so it is the same vector. Only the starting point differs.
$(2,-1,4)$ has 3 components, so it is an arrow in 3-D: 2 along x, 1 backwards along y, 4 along z.
A vector with 5 components lives in $\mathbb R^5$. You cannot draw it, but every rule still works.
examples.answer: Yes, the same vector; and $(2,-1,4)\in\mathbb R^3$.

cards.why: Vectors are the basic objects of linear algebra and of machine learning (a data point, a list of weights, a gradient). If a vector is only a list to you, geometry questions feel random. If it is only an arrow, you cannot compute. In GATE: points and directions in $\mathbb R^2$ and $\mathbb R^3$, and coordinate vectors in linear algebra questions.
how: Read each component as 'how far along this direction'.
For the vector from $P$ to $Q$, compute $Q-P$.
Count the components to find the dimension. Two vectors can only be compared or combined when the dimensions match.
In $\mathbb R^2$, sketch the arrow: a rough picture catches sign mistakes.
cards.mistake: Swapping the order of components or the direction of the subtraction. $\overrightarrow{PQ}=Q-P$, not $P-Q$ (that is $\overrightarrow{QP}$, the arrow in the opposite direction). And $(3,2)\ne(2,3)$.
edge_cases: The zero vector is the arrow that goes nowhere: all components are 0.
A vector with one component, $(5)$, is just a number on a line.
A row $(3,2)$ and a column $\begin{bmatrix}3\\2\end{bmatrix}$ hold the same numbers. Matrix multiplication will care which shape you use.
Vectors with different numbers of components are never equal.
connections: Used in: Linear algebra. Vector spaces, span and independence are all about lists of numbers viewed as arrows.
Used in: Machine learning. A data point with $n$ features is a vector in $\mathbb R^n$, and k-nearest neighbours measures distances between such vectors.
Used in: Geometry. Points, directions and displacements are vectors.

check.q: Write the vector for '5 steps left and 2 steps up'.
How many components does $(1,0,4,2)$ have, and where does it live?
check.a: 4 components, so it is a vector in $\mathbb R^4$.

cards.title: Adding and scaling vectors
cards.simple: Adding two vectors is like walking two legs of a trip. Walk the first arrow, then start where you ended up and walk the second. The straight arrow from your starting point to your final position is the sum. With lists you do it number by number: (2,1) + (1,3) = (3,4). Scaling means stretching: doubling every number makes the arrow twice as long in the same direction, and multiplying by a negative number makes it point the other way. In exam words: vector addition is component-wise, scalar multiplication multiplies every component by the same number, and something like 2u + 3v is called a linear combination.
cards.idea: To **add** vectors, add matching components. Picture it as walking one arrow, then the other from where you stopped. To **scale** a vector by a number $c$, multiply every component by $c$: the arrow stretches ($c>1$), shrinks ($0<c<1$) or flips ($c<0$). Mixing both gives combinations such as $2u+3v$.
cards.definition:
$$u+v=(u_1+v_1,\;u_2+v_2,\dots)\qquad cu=(cu_1,\;cu_2,\dots)$$

$u$ and $v$ must have the same number of components. $c$ is an ordinary number called a **scalar**. Subtraction is addition of a flipped vector: $u-v=u+(-1)v$, component by component. A **linear combination** is any $au+bv$ with scalars $a$ and $b$.
cards.intuition_full: Adding arrows tip to tail works because each arrow is a move. Move by $u$, then move by $v$: the total move is the sum. The order does not matter ($u+v=v+u$) because the two routes form a parallelogram and meet at the same corner. Scaling keeps the direction (or exactly reverses it) and changes only the length, so all multiples of one vector sit on one line through the origin. Take two arrows that do not point along the same line and the combinations $au+bv$ can reach every point of the plane. That idea, how much of each arrow you mix, is the whole of 'span' and 'basis' in linear algebra. It is also how a prediction like $0.5\times\text{area}+3\times\text{rooms}$ is built in machine learning.

steps: Slide a copy of $v$ so its tail sits on the tip of $u$. It now ends at $(2+1,\,1+3)$.
The arrow from the origin to that end point is $u+v=(3,4)$: add matching components.
Scaling: $2u=(2\cdot2,\,2\cdot1)=(4,2)$, an arrow twice as long in the same direction.

examples.setup: What is $u+(-u)$? And what is $(1,2)+(1,2,3)$?
steps: $-u$ is $u$ scaled by $-1$: it points the opposite way.
Adding, each component cancels, so $u+(-u)=(0,0)$, the zero vector. The walk ends where it started.
$(1,2)$ has 2 components and $(1,2,3)$ has 3. There is no third component to add to, so the sum is **not defined**.
examples.answer: The zero vector, and 'undefined' for mismatched sizes.

cards.why: Addition and scaling are the two operations that define a vector space. Everything in linear algebra (span, independence, solving $Ax=b$) is built from them. In GATE: computing combinations like $2u-v$, checking whether a vector is a combination of others, and geometry in $\mathbb R^2$.
how: Check that both vectors have the same number of components.
Add or subtract component by component.
Scale every component by the same number, watching the signs.
For a linear combination, scale first, then add.
cards.mistake: Scaling only one component, or fumbling a double negative. $3u$ multiplies **every** component, and $12-(-4)$ is $16$, not $8$.
edge_cases: Scaling by 0 gives the zero vector.
Scaling by $-1$ reverses the arrow.
$u+v=v+u$, but $u-v\ne v-u$ (they are opposites).
Adding vectors of different sizes is undefined.
connections: Used in: Linear algebra. Span, linear independence and bases are about combinations $au+bv$.
Used in: Machine learning. A gradient descent update is $w\leftarrow w-\eta\,\nabla L$: a vector minus a scaled vector.
Used in: Geometry. Midpoints and displacements are sums and halves of vectors.

check.a: Yes: $0\cdot(1,2)+0\cdot(3,4)=(0,0)$. The zero combination always works.

cards.title: Length of a vector
cards.simple: The length of an arrow is how far you travel in a straight line. For the vector (3,4) you walk 3 across and 4 up, which makes a right-angled triangle, and the straight path is its longest side. Pythagoras gives the length: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25, and the square root of 25 is 5. Longer vectors work the same way: square every number, add them up, take the square root. A vector with length 1 is called a unit vector, and you make one by dividing a vector by its own length. In exam words: the length (norm) is |v| = √(v₁² + v₂² + ...), and v/|v| is the unit vector.
cards.idea: The **length** (or norm) of a vector is the distance from the origin to its tip. Move $v_1$ across and $v_2$ up and you have a right-angled triangle, so Pythagoras gives the length. The vector $(3,4)$ has length $\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=\sqrt{25}=5$. Dividing a vector by its length gives a **unit vector** of length 1 with the same direction.
cards.definition:
$$|v|=\sqrt{v_1^2+v_2^2+\cdots+v_n^2}\qquad \hat v=\frac{v}{|v|}$$

$|v|$ is the length of $v$ (the positive square root). $\hat v$ ('v hat') is the unit vector in the direction of $v$, defined when $v\ne\mathbf0$. The distance between points $A$ and $B$ is $|B-A|$. Scaling: $|cv|=|c|\,|v|$.
cards.intuition_full: In 2-D the legs of the triangle are the components, so Pythagoras applies directly: $|v|^2=v_1^2+v_2^2$. In 3-D apply Pythagoras twice: first across the floor, then up. $\sqrt{v_1^2+v_2^2}$ is the length along the floor, and the full length is $\sqrt{(\text{floor})^2+v_3^2}$. The same pattern continues in any dimension. Squaring removes the signs, so $(-3,4)$ has the same length as $(3,4)$: going left or right does not change how far you walk. Notice that $|v|^2=v\cdot v$, so length is a dot product in disguise. That link comes in the next card. The distance between two points is the length of the vector between them, which is how k-nearest neighbours decides who is 'close'.

examples.setup: Find the length of $v=(3,4)$, then make a unit vector in its direction.
steps: Draw $v=(3,4)$ and its two legs: 3 across and 4 up. They form a right-angled triangle.
Divide each component by 5: $\hat v=(0.6,\,0.8)$, which has length $\sqrt{0.36+0.64}=1$.

examples.setup: Find the distance between $A=(2,5)$ and $B=(8,13)$.
examples.answer: 10. Subtract first, then take the length. (Shortcut: $(6,8)=2\times(3,4)$, so the length is $2\times5$.)

steps: Negating every component squares away the signs: $|(-2,-3,-6)|=7$ too.
$|(1,1)|=\sqrt2\approx1.414$: lengths are not always whole numbers.

cards.why: Length measures size and distance: the size of an error in regression, closeness in k-nearest neighbours, and the check for unit vectors in projections and orthogonal bases. In GATE: lengths and distances in $\mathbb R^2$ and $\mathbb R^3$, normalising a vector, and expressions like $|u+v|^2$.
how: Square each component.
Add the squares.
Take the positive square root.
For the distance between points, subtract first.
To make a unit vector, divide every component by the length.
cards.mistake: Forgetting the square root (answering 25 instead of 5), or adding the components first: $|(3,4)|$ is $5$, not $3+4=7$. Also, $|u+v|\ne|u|+|v|$ in general.
edge_cases: Only the zero vector has length 0.
The distance from $A$ to $B$ equals the distance from $B$ to $A$.
The length of $(a,0)$ is $|a|$: on an axis, length is the absolute value.
connections: Used in: Linear algebra. Orthonormal bases, projection and Gram-Schmidt need lengths and unit vectors.
Used in: Machine learning. k-nearest neighbours and k-means use the length of the difference between vectors, and ridge regression penalises $|w|^2$.
Used in: Geometry. The distance between two points in the plane is a vector length.

2. Pythagoras: length$^2=3^2+4^2$, and $3^2=9$, $4^2=16$.

4. Length $=\sqrt{25}=5$.
5. Divide each component by 5: $\hat v=(0.6,\,0.8)$, which has length $\sqrt{0.36+0.64}=1$.

**Answer:** $|v|=5$ and $\hat v=(0.6,0.8)$.

cards.title: The dot product
cards.simple: The dot product tells you how much two lists 'agree'. Multiply the first numbers together, then the second numbers, then the third, and add all those products into one number. For (2,5,1) and (3,0,4): 2×3 = 6, 5×0 = 0, 1×4 = 4, and the total is 10. You get a single number, not a new arrow. If the two arrows point roughly the same way the answer is large and positive. If they point in opposite directions it is negative. If they meet at a right angle it is exactly zero. In exam words: u·v is the sum of the products uᵢvᵢ, and u·v = 0 exactly when u and v are perpendicular (orthogonal).
cards.idea: The **dot product** of two same-size vectors multiplies matching components and adds the results. The answer is a **single number**. It is positive when the arrows point in a similar direction, negative when they point apart, and **zero when they are perpendicular**. A vector dotted with itself gives its squared length.
cards.definition:
$$u\cdot v=u_1v_1+u_2v_2+\cdots+u_nv_n=|u|\,|v|\cos\theta$$

$u_iv_i$ are the products of matching components. $\theta$ is the angle between the two arrows (between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$). Special cases: $u\cdot u=|u|^2$, and $u\cdot v=0$ with both vectors non-zero means $\theta=90^\circ$. The angle comes from $\cos\theta=\dfrac{u\cdot v}{|u|\,|v|}$.
cards.intuition_full: The sum of products is a score of agreement. Where both vectors have large components with the same sign, you add a big positive amount. Where they have opposite signs, you subtract. A zero component in either vector contributes nothing, which is why $(1,0)\cdot(0,1)=0$: the x-arrow and y-arrow share nothing. The cosine form $|u||v|\cos\theta$ says the same thing geometrically: it multiplies the length of $u$ by the length of the part of $v$ that points along $u$. When $\theta=90^\circ$ there is no part along $u$, and $\cos90^\circ=0$. Both forms are equal, so use whichever fits: components when you have numbers, the cosine when you have lengths and an angle. Dot products answer 'is this perpendicular', 'what is the angle' and 'how similar are these two lists', and in the next cards they become the building block of matrix products.

examples.setup: Compute $u\cdot v$ for $u=(2,5,1)$ and $v=(3,0,4)$.
steps: Line up the two lists, matching components in the same column.

examples.setup: For which $k$ are $(3,k)$ and $(4,6)$ perpendicular?
steps: Perpendicular means the dot product is 0.

examples.setup: For $u=(3,0)$, find the angle it makes with $v=(2,2)$ and with $w=(-2,2)$.
steps: A negative dot product means the angle is more than $90^\circ$: the arrows point apart.

cards.why: The dot product is how linear algebra measures angles, perpendicularity and projections, and in machine learning it is the prediction step ($w\cdot x$) of linear models and of every neuron. In GATE: orthogonality tests, finding an unknown so that two vectors are perpendicular, and the cosine of an angle.
how: Check that the vectors have the same number of components.
Multiply matching components.
Add all the products: the result is one number.
For 'perpendicular', set the dot product equal to 0 and solve.
For an angle, divide by both lengths to get $\cos\theta$.
cards.mistake: Leaving the products as a list instead of adding them, which confuses the dot product with component-wise multiplication. $(2,5,1)\cdot(3,0,4)$ is the number $10$, not the vector $(6,0,4)$.
edge_cases: $u\cdot v=v\cdot u$: the order does not matter.
$u\cdot u=|u|^2\ge0$, and it equals 0 only for the zero vector.
The zero vector is perpendicular to everything, since its dot product with anything is 0.
Two vectors with dot product 0 are called orthogonal.
connections: Used in: Linear algebra. Orthogonality, projection and inner product spaces all start with $u\cdot v$.
Used in: Machine learning. A linear model predicts with $w\cdot x$, and cosine similarity is $\frac{u\cdot v}{|u||v|}$.
Used in: Matrices. Every entry of a matrix product is a dot product of a row and a column; that is the next two cards.

It is positive when the arrows point in a similar direction, negative when they point apart, and **zero when they are perpendicular**. A vector dotted with itself gives its squared length.

$$u\cdot v=u_1v_1+u_2v_2+\cdots+u_nv_n=|u|\,|v|\cos\theta$$

$u_iv_i$ are the products of matching components. $\theta$ is the angle between the two arrows (between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$). Special cases: $u\cdot u=|u|^2$, and $u\cdot v=0$ with both vectors non-zero means $\theta=90^\circ$. The angle comes from $\cos\theta=\dfrac{u\cdot v}{|u|\,|v|}$.

**Worked example.** Compute $u\cdot v$ for $u=(2,5,1)$ and $v=(3,0,4)$.

1. Line up the two lists, matching components in the same column.
2. First pair: $2\times3=6$.
3. Second pair: $5\times0=0$.
4. Third pair: $1\times4=4$.
5. Add the products: $6+0+4=10$. One number.

**Answer:** $u\cdot v=10$.
cards.why_full:
The dot product is how linear algebra measures angles, perpendicularity and projections, and in machine learning it is the prediction step ($w\cdot x$) of linear models and of every neuron. In GATE: orthogonality tests, finding an unknown so that two vectors are perpendicular, and the cosine of an angle.

Foundation, used in: la.vecspace, la.proj, ml.knn, ml.linreg.
cards.trap: Leaving the products as a list instead of adding them, which confuses the dot product with component-wise multiplication. $(2,5,1)\cdot(3,0,4)$ is the number $10$, not the vector $(6,0,4)$.

cards.title: Matrix times vector
cards.simple: A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers. To multiply a matrix by a vector, take each row of the grid, line it up with the vector, and do a dot product. Each row gives one number, and those numbers stack up into the answer. Think of shopping: each row of the grid is the price list of one shop, and the vector says how many of each item you buy. Each row's dot product is your bill at that shop. The vector must have as many entries as the grid has columns, or the rows will not line up. In exam words: for an m × n matrix A and a vector x with n entries, Ax has m entries, and the i-th entry is (row i of A) · x.
cards.idea: A **matrix** is a grid of numbers with rows and columns. To multiply a matrix $A$ by a vector $x$, take each **row** of $A$, dot it with $x$, and write the results one under another. A matrix with 2 rows and 3 columns turns a 3-number vector into a 2-number vector. You can also see $Ax$ as a **mix of the columns** of $A$, using the entries of $x$ as the amounts.
cards.definition:
$$(Ax)_i=(\text{row }i\text{ of }A)\cdot x=a_{i1}x_1+a_{i2}x_2+\cdots+a_{in}x_n$$

$A$ has $m$ rows and $n$ columns (an $m\times n$ matrix; rows first), and $a_{ij}$ is the entry in row $i$, column $j$. The vector $x$ must have $n$ entries, and then $Ax$ has $m$ entries. Column view: $Ax=x_1(\text{col }1)+x_2(\text{col }2)+\cdots+x_n(\text{col }n)$.
cards.intuition_full: Think of $A$ as a machine that takes a vector in and gives a vector out. Each row of $A$ is one recipe that reads the input and produces one number. Row 1 makes output 1, row 2 makes output 2. That is why the number of rows decides the output size, and the number of columns must match the input size. The column view says the same thing differently: the output is built from $x_1$ copies of column 1, $x_2$ copies of column 2, and so on, added together. Both views give identical numbers, so use whichever is easier. When you see $Ax=b$ in linear algebra, it is a system of equations, with one equation per row. In machine learning, one layer of a neural network is exactly $Wx+b$.

examples.setup: $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0&1\\1&3&2\end{bmatrix}$ and $x=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{bmatrix}$. Find $Ax$.
steps: $A$ is $2\times3$ and $x$ has 3 entries, so $Ax$ exists and has 2 entries.

examples.setup: $A=\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\2&0\\1&4\end{bmatrix}$ and $x=(2,5)$. Find $Ax$ and say how many entries it has.
steps: $A$ is $3\times2$ and $x$ has 2 entries, so the product is defined and has 3 entries.

examples.setup: Using the $2\times3$ matrix $A$ from the first example, what is $A(0,1,0)$? And can $A$ multiply $(1,2)$?
steps: So $A(0,1,0)=(0,3)$, which is column 2 of $A$. A vector with a single 1 picks out one column.
$(1,2)$ has 2 entries but $A$ has 3 columns: the rows do not line up, so $A(1,2)$ is **not defined**.

cards.why: Matrix-vector products are how linear equations, linear maps and neural-network layers are written. In GATE: computing $Ax$ for a small $A$, writing a system as $Ax=b$, and eigenvalue questions where $Ax=\lambda x$.
how: Check the sizes: columns of $A$ must equal the entries of $x$.
Take row 1 and dot it with $x$; that is output 1.
Repeat for every row.
Stack the results into a column. The output has as many entries as $A$ has rows.
cards.mistake: Dotting columns of $A$ with $x$ instead of rows, or ignoring the size rule. A $2\times3$ matrix cannot multiply a 2-entry vector. The pattern is left matrix by rows, right vector as is.
edge_cases: $Ax$ with $x=\mathbf0$ is always the zero vector.
A vector with a single 1 and 0s elsewhere picks out one column of $A$.
A $1\times n$ matrix times $x$ is just a dot product (one number).
$A(cx)=c\,Ax$ and $A(x+y)=Ax+Ay$: that is what 'linear' means.
connections: Used in: Linear algebra. A system of equations is $Ax=b$, eigenvectors satisfy $Ax=\lambda x$, and rank counts independent columns.
Used in: Machine learning. A layer computes $Wx+b$, and linear regression predicts $Xw$ for all rows of data at once.
Used in: Computer graphics. Rotating or scaling a point is a matrix-vector product.

check.q: Can a $3\times4$ matrix multiply a vector with 3 entries?
check.a: No. The vector needs 4 entries, one per column.
Row 1: $6$. Row 2: $7$. The result is $(6,7)$ again.

A **matrix** is a grid of numbers with rows and columns. To multiply a matrix $A$ by a vector $x$, take each **row** of $A$, dot it with $x$, and write the results one under another. A matrix with 2 rows and 3 columns turns a 3-number vector into a 2-number vector. You can also see $Ax$ as a **mix of the columns** of $A$, using the entries of $x$ as the amounts.

$$(Ax)_i=(\text{row }i\text{ of }A)\cdot x=a_{i1}x_1+a_{i2}x_2+\cdots+a_{in}x_n$$

$A$ has $m$ rows and $n$ columns (an $m\times n$ matrix; rows first), and $a_{ij}$ is the entry in row $i$, column $j$. The vector $x$ must have $n$ entries, and then $Ax$ has $m$ entries. Column view: $Ax=x_1(\text{col }1)+x_2(\text{col }2)+\cdots+x_n(\text{col }n)$.

1. $A$ is $2\times3$ and $x$ has 3 entries, so $Ax$ exists and has 2 entries.
2. Row 1 of $A$ with $x$: $2\cdot1+0\cdot2+1\cdot3=5$.
3. Row 2 of $A$ with $x$: $1\cdot1+3\cdot2+2\cdot3=1+6+6=13$.
4. Column check: $1\cdot(2,1)+2\cdot(0,3)+3\cdot(1,2)=(2,1)+(0,6)+(3,6)=(5,13)$.

**Answer:** $Ax=(5,13)$.

cards.title: Matrix times matrix
cards.simple: To multiply two matrices, do the matrix-times-vector trick once for each column of the second matrix. The entry in row i, column j of the answer comes from row i of the left matrix and column j of the right matrix: multiply pairs and add. Run one finger along the row and another down the column. Each row and column pair makes exactly one number in the answer. The left matrix's number of columns must equal the right matrix's number of rows. Unlike ordinary numbers, the order matters: A × B is usually not B × A. In exam words: (m×n)(n×p) = m×p, entry (i,j) of AB is row i of A dotted with column j of B, and AB ≠ BA in general.
cards.idea: To multiply matrices $A$ and $B$, fill the answer one entry at a time: the entry in **row $i$, column $j$** is the dot product of **row $i$ of $A$** with **column $j$ of $B$**. This only works when that row and that column have the same length. Matrix multiplication is **not commutative**: usually $AB\ne BA$.
cards.definition:
$$(AB)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_{ik}\,b_{kj}\qquad(m\times n)(n\times p)=m\times p$$

$a_{ik}$ is the entry in row $i$, column $k$ of $A$, and $b_{kj}$ is the entry in row $k$, column $j$ of $B$. The two **inner** sizes ($n$ and $n$) must match, and the two **outer** sizes give the size of the answer. The symbol $\sum$ means 'add up' (here over $k=1$ to $n$), so each entry is just a dot product.
cards.intuition_full: A product of matrices means 'apply $B$ first, then $A$'. Each column of $B$ is a vector, and $A$ transforms it by the matrix-vector rule from the previous card, so the columns of $AB$ are $A$ times each column of $B$. That is why the inner sizes must match: the number of columns of $A$ must equal the length of the columns of $B$. The size rule, rows of $A$ by columns of $B$, tells you the shape of the answer before you compute a single entry, which is a good exam check. Order matters because 'rotate then stretch' differs from 'stretch then rotate'. With sizes alone, $AB$ may exist while $BA$ does not, or $BA$ may have a different size. A quick sanity check on your work: an $m\times p$ answer has $m\times p$ entries, and each one is a dot product of $n$ pairs.

examples.setup: $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&0\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&4\end{bmatrix}$. Find $AB$.
steps: Sizes: $(2\times2)(2\times2)$. The inner sizes match, so $AB$ exists and is $2\times2$: four entries to fill.

examples.setup: $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1&0\\1&3&1\end{bmatrix}$ ($2\times3$) and $B=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\\4&0\end{bmatrix}$ ($3\times2$). Find $AB$ and the sum of its diagonal entries.
steps: Sizes: $(2\times3)(3\times2)$. The inner 3 and 3 match, so the product is $2\times2$.

examples.setup: For the matrices of the first example, find $BA$. For the matrices of the second example, what size is $BA$?
steps: Entry (1,1) of $BA$: row 1 of $B$ with column 1 of $A$: $2\cdot1+1\cdot3=5$.
In the second example, $BA$ is $(3\times2)(2\times3)=3\times3$, not even the same size as $AB$.

cards.why: Matrix products combine operations: apply one transformation, then another. They appear in systems of equations, determinants, eigenvalue problems and every neural network. In GATE: computing one entry or the full product of small matrices, deciding whether a product exists and what size it is, and powers like $A^2$.
how: Write the sizes and check that the inner numbers match.
The answer's size is (rows of $A$) by (columns of $B$).
For entry $(i,j)$, run along row $i$ of $A$ and down column $j$ of $B$, multiply the pairs and add.
Fill the answer entry by entry, and check one entry twice.
cards.mistake: Multiplying matching positions ($a_{ij}b_{ij}$) as if matrices multiply entry by entry, or assuming $AB=BA$. The matrix product is row times column, and the order is part of the answer.
edge_cases: If $AB$ exists, $BA$ may not exist or may have a different size.
Even for square matrices, $AB\ne BA$ in general.
$A^2$ only exists for a square $A$.
$AB=0$ does not force $A=0$ or $B=0$: for example $\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$.
connections: Used in: Linear algebra. Determinants of products, matrix powers, LU factorisation and eigenvalue problems all multiply matrices.
Used in: Machine learning. Stacked layers are products of weight matrices, and PCA works with $X^TX$.
Used in: Graphs. Powers of an adjacency matrix count walks.

check.q: $A$ is $2\times4$ and $B$ is $4\times5$. What size is $AB$?
Do $A$ ($3\times2$) and $B$ ($3\times2$) multiply, in the order $AB$?
check.a: No: the inner sizes 2 and 3 do not match.

cards.asked: Foundation, used in: la.matrices_det, la.lu, la.eigen, ml.ffnn.

steps: Sizes: $(2\times2)(2\times2)$. The inner sizes match, so $AB$ exists and is $2\times2$: four entries to fill.

cards.what_full:
To multiply matrices $A$ and $B$, fill the answer one entry at a time: the entry in **row $i$, column $j$** is the dot product of **row $i$ of $A$** with **column $j$ of $B$**. This only works when that row and that column have the same length. Matrix multiplication is **not commutative**: usually $AB\ne BA$.

$$(AB)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_{ik}\,b_{kj}\qquad(m\times n)(n\times p)=m\times p$$

$a_{ik}$ is the entry in row $i$, column $k$ of $A$, and $b_{kj}$ is the entry in row $k$, column $j$ of $B$. The two **inner** sizes ($n$ and $n$) must match, and the two **outer** sizes give the size of the answer. The symbol $\sum$ means 'add up' (here over $k=1$ to $n$), so each entry is just a dot product.

**Worked example.** $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&0\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&4\end{bmatrix}$. Find $AB$.

1. Sizes: $(2\times2)(2\times2)$. The inner sizes match, so $AB$ exists and is $2\times2$: four entries to fill.
2. Row 1 of $A$ with column 1 of $B$: $1\cdot2+2\cdot0=2$.
3. Row 1 of $A$ with column 2 of $B$: $1\cdot1+2\cdot4=9$.
4. Row 2 of $A$ with column 1 of $B$: $3\cdot2+0\cdot0=6$.
5. Row 2 of $A$ with column 2 of $B$: $3\cdot1+0\cdot4=3$.

**Answer:** $AB=\begin{bmatrix}2&9\\6&3\end{bmatrix}$.

In GATE: computing one entry or the full product of small matrices, deciding whether a product exists and what size it is, and powers like $A^2$.

Foundation, used in: la.matrices_det, la.lu, la.eigen, ml.ffnn.
cards.trap: Multiplying matching positions ($a_{ij}b_{ij}$) as if matrices multiply entry by entry, or assuming $AB=BA$. The matrix product is row times column, and the order is part of the answer.

cards.title: Identity and transpose
cards.simple: Two small special moves. The identity matrix is the 'times 1' of matrices: it has 1s down the diagonal and 0s everywhere else, and multiplying by it changes nothing, just as 5 × 1 = 5. The transpose flips a grid over its main diagonal, so the first row becomes the first column, the second row becomes the second column, and so on. A grid with 2 rows and 3 columns turns into one with 3 rows and 2 columns. Flip it twice and you are back where you started. In exam words: IA = AI = A, (Aᵀ)ᵀ = A, and (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ with the order reversed.
cards.idea: The **identity matrix** $I$ has 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere, and $IA=AI=A$: it does nothing, like multiplying by 1. The **transpose** $A^T$ turns rows into columns: entry $(i,j)$ of $A$ becomes entry $(j,i)$ of $A^T$. A $2\times3$ matrix becomes $3\times2$.
cards.definition:
$$I_3=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}$$

$$(A^T)_{ij}=A_{ji},\qquad (AB)^T=B^TA^T$$

$I_n$ is the $n\times n$ identity (shown for $n=3$). For $A$ of size $m\times n$, use $I_m$ on the left and $I_n$ on the right. $(A^T)_{ij}=A_{ji}$ means: swap the row and column numbers. Rules: $(A^T)^T=A$, $(A+B)^T=A^T+B^T$, and the transpose of a product reverses the order. A matrix with $A^T=A$ is called **symmetric**.
cards.intuition_full: The identity makes each output entry copy the matching input: row $i$ of $I$ is zero except for a 1 in position $i$, so its dot product with $x$ picks out $x_i$ and nothing else. That is why $Ix=x$. For the transpose, picture a mirror along the main diagonal (top-left to bottom-right): the entry at row 2, column 3 swaps places with the entry at row 3, column 2, and entries on the diagonal stay put. A symmetric matrix looks the same in the mirror. The order reversal for products has a size reason. If $A$ is $2\times3$ and $B$ is $3\times4$, then $AB$ is $2\times4$, so $(AB)^T$ is $4\times2$. $B^T$ is $4\times3$ and $A^T$ is $3\times2$, so only $B^TA^T$ has matching inner sizes; $A^TB^T$ would be $(3\times2)(4\times3)$ and does not even exist. In machine learning the transpose turns a column of features into a row, so $x^Tx$ is a dot product.

examples.setup: Transpose $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\end{bmatrix}$, then check that $I_2A=A$.
steps: $A$ has 2 rows and 3 columns, so its size is $2\times3$.
The 6 sat in row 2, column 3 of $A$. In $A^T$ it sits in row 3, column 2, and the size is now $3\times2$.
Identity: $I_2=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$. Row 1 of $I_2$ dotted with each column of $A$ picks the top entry: 1, 2, 3.
Row 2 of $I_2$ picks the bottom entries 4, 5, 6. So $I_2A=A$, unchanged.

examples.setup: With $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&0\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&4\end{bmatrix}$ (so $AB=\begin{bmatrix}2&9\\6&3\end{bmatrix}$), verify that $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$ and that $A^TB^T$ is different.
steps: $B^TA^T$: entries $2\cdot1+0\cdot2=2$, $2\cdot3+0\cdot0=6$, $1\cdot1+4\cdot2=9$, $1\cdot3+4\cdot0=3$. That gives $\begin{bmatrix}2&6\\9&3\end{bmatrix}$, the same as $(AB)^T$.
$A^TB^T$: entry (1,1) is $1\cdot2+3\cdot1=5$, and the full product is $\begin{bmatrix}5&12\\4&0\end{bmatrix}$, which is different.

examples.setup: $A$ is $2\times3$. What size of identity multiplies it on the left, and on the right? Is $S=\begin{bmatrix}2&7\\7&5\end{bmatrix}$ symmetric?
steps: On the left, $IA$ needs the inner sizes to match, so $I$ must be $2\times2$: $I_2A=A$.
On the right, $AI$ needs $I$ to be $3\times3$: $AI_3=A$.
So the identity's size depends on the side. $I_3A$ is not even defined.
$S^T$: swap entries (1,2) and (2,1). Both are 7, so $S^T=S$. Yes, $S$ is symmetric.
examples.answer: $I_2$ on the left, $I_3$ on the right; $S$ is symmetric.

cards.why: These two make matrix algebra work. The identity is the 'one' that inverses are defined against, and the transpose appears in symmetric matrices, orthogonal matrices, $A^TA$ and least squares. In GATE: finding entries of $A^T$, using $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$, and recognising symmetric matrices.
how: To transpose, write each row of $A$ as a column of $A^T$.
Check the size: an $m\times n$ matrix has an $n\times m$ transpose.
In $(AB)^T$, reverse the order: $B^TA^T$.
For $IA$ or $AI$, match the identity's size to the side it sits on.
cards.mistake: Writing $(AB)^T=A^TB^T$ in the same order. The order reverses: $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$. Other slips are transposing only part of the grid, or putting an identity of the wrong size next to a non-square $A$.
edge_cases: The diagonal of a matrix does not change under the transpose.
A symmetric matrix satisfies $A^T=A$ and must be square.
The transpose of a column vector is a row vector, so $x^Tx$ is a $1\times1$ number, namely $|x|^2$.
connections: Used in: Linear algebra. Inverses ($A^{-1}A=I$), symmetric and orthogonal matrices ($Q^TQ=I$) and eigenvalues of symmetric matrices all rely on these two ideas.
Used in: Machine learning. Least squares uses $(X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty$, and covariance matrices are symmetric.
Used in: Graphs. An undirected graph has a symmetric adjacency matrix.

check.q: What is the size of $A^T$ if $A$ is $4\times1$?

check.a: Yes: the identity equals its own transpose.

$$I_3=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}$$

scenes.title: The vector (3, 2) as an arrow and as a list

steps.caption: The vector $v=(3,2)$ says: start at the origin and go 3 steps right.
Then go 2 steps up from where you are.
The straight arrow from the origin to where you ended up is the vector $v$.
As a list it is $[3,\,2]$: the same information as the arrow, written as numbers.

scenes.title: Adding vectors tip to tail, and scaling

steps.caption: Draw $u=(2,1)$ and $v=(1,3)$ from the origin.
Slide a copy of $v$ so that its tail sits on the tip of $u$. It now ends at $(2+1,\,1+3)$.
The arrow from the origin to that end point is $u+v=(3,4)$. Add matching components.
Scaling: $2u=(2\cdot2,\,2\cdot1)=(4,2)$ is an arrow twice as long in the same direction.
Draw $v=(3,4)$ with its two legs: 3 across and 4 up. They form a right-angled triangle.
Pythagoras: length$^2$ = $3^2+4^2$. The squares are 9 and 16.
Add the squares: $9+16=25$.
Length $=\sqrt{25}=5$.
Divide each component by 5. The unit vector $(0.6,\,0.8)$ points the same way and has length 1.

scenes.title: Dot product: multiply pairs, then add

steps.caption: Line up $u$ and $v$ so matching components sit in the same column.
First pair: $2\times3=6$.
Second pair: $5\times0=0$.
Third pair: $1\times4=4$.
Add the products: $6+0+4=10$. The dot product is a single number, not a list.

scenes.title: Matrix times vector: one dot product per row

steps.caption: $A$ is $2\times3$ and $x$ has 3 entries, so $Ax$ exists and has 2 entries: one per row of $A$.
Row 1 of $A$ dotted with $x$: $2\cdot1+0\cdot2+1\cdot3=5$. That is the first entry.
Row 2 of $A$ dotted with $x$: $1\cdot1+3\cdot2+2\cdot3=1+6+6=13$.
Column check: $Ax$ is also $1$ copy of column 1, $2$ copies of column 2 and $3$ copies of column 3, added up.

scenes.title: Matrix times matrix: row by column

steps.caption: Sizes first: the inner sizes (2 and 2) match, so $AB$ exists and is $2\times2$. Four entries to fill.
Entry (1,1): row 1 of $A$ with column 1 of $B$: $1\cdot2+2\cdot0=2$.
Entry (1,2): row 1 of $A$ with column 2 of $B$: $1\cdot1+2\cdot4=9$.
Entry (2,1): row 2 of $A$ with column 1 of $B$: $3\cdot2+0\cdot0=6$.
Entry (2,2): row 2 of $A$ with column 2 of $B$: $3\cdot1+0\cdot4=3$.
Swap the order and you get a different matrix: $BA=\begin{bmatrix}5&4\\12&0\end{bmatrix}$, not $AB$. Order matters.

scenes.title: Transpose flips rows to columns; the identity changes nothing

steps.caption: $A$ has 2 rows and 3 columns, so its size is $2\times3$.
Row 1 of $A$, $(1,2,3)$, becomes column 1 of $A^T$.
Row 2, $(4,5,6)$, becomes column 2. Now $A^T$ is complete, and its size is $3\times2$.
The 6 sat in row 2, column 3 of $A$. In $A^T$ it sits in row 3, column 2: the row and column numbers swap.

set.text: (2,3) in A moves to (3,2) in Aᵀ

steps.caption: Identity: $I_2$ has 1s on the diagonal. Row 1 of $I_2$ dotted with each column of $A$ picks out the top entry: 1, 2, 3.

set.text: row 1 of I picks row 1 of A

steps.caption: Row 2 of $I_2$ picks the bottom entries 4, 5, 6. So $I_2A=A$: nothing changed.
